questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bullet, fired into a door gets embedded exactly at it's centre, causing the door to rotate about it's vertical axis, practically without friction, with an angular velocity of $0.625\ rads^{-1}$. The door is 1.0 m wide and weighs 12 kg. If the mass of the bullet is 10g, find the speed with which it was fired. (Hint: The moment of inertia of the door about the vertical axis at one end is $\dfrac{ML^2}{3}$).
questions.solution:
By conservation of angular momentum about the vertical axis of the door:

$L_i = L_f$

$m v r = (I_{door} + I_{bullet}) \omega$

$m v \left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right) = \left(\dfrac{ML^2}{3} + m\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)^2\right) \omega$

Substituting the given values $M = 12\ kg$, $L = 1.0\ m$, $m = 0.01\ kg$, and $\omega = 0.625\ rads^{-1}$:

$0.01 \times v \times 0.5 = \left(\dfrac{12 \times 1^2}{3} + 0.01 \times 0.5^2\right) \times 0.625$

$0.005 v = (4 + 0.0025) \times 0.625$

Neglecting the small term $0.0025$ compared to $4$:

$0.005 v = 4 \times 0.625$

$0.005 v = 2.5$

$v = \dfrac{2.5}{0.005} = 500\ ms^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A singer, during his performance, stands on the edge of a circular turntable, and begins to walk along its edge with a speed of $1.5\ ms^{-1}$ relative to the ground. The turn table is mounted on a frictionless vertical axle. Its radius R = 3m and its moment of inertia about the axle is 150 kg m². It is initially at rest. If the mass of the singer is 75kg, the time taken by the man to complete one revolution is:
questions.solution:
Given:
Speed of the singer relative to the ground, $v = 1.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$
Radius of the circular turntable, $R = 3\text{ m}$

The problem asks for the time taken by the singer to complete one revolution. Since the speed of the singer is given relative to the ground, the time taken to complete one revolution relative to the ground can be calculated directly using the circumference of the circular path.

The total distance covered in one revolution is $2\pi R$.

Time taken $T = \dfrac{2\pi R}{v}$

Substituting the given values:
$T = \dfrac{2\pi \times 3}{1.5}$

$T = 4\pi$

$T = 4 \times 3.1416 \approx 12.57\text{ s}$

The mass of the singer and the moment of inertia of the turntable are extraneous information provided as distractors, as the ground speed is already explicitly given.

Answer: $12.57$s

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle starts rotating from rest. The instantaneous angular displacement is $\theta = 3t^3 - t^2$, where $\theta$ is in radian and t in s; The angular velocity at $t = 1$ s is
questions.solution:
The angular displacement is given by $\theta = 3t^3 - t^2$.

The angular velocity $\omega$ is the rate of change of angular displacement with respect to time, given by $\omega = \dfrac{d\theta}{dt}$.

Differentiating $\theta$ with respect to $t$:

$\omega = \dfrac{d}{dt}(3t^3 - t^2) = 9t^2 - 2t$

Substituting $t = 1$ s:

$\omega = 9(1)^2 - 2(1) = 7 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$

Answer: $7\ rads^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $Four masses each 2 kg are placed at the corners A, B, C, D of a mass less square frame. 40 kg mass is at the centre O of a square frame of side 0.2m. It is to be rotated about an axis passing through the centre O and perpendicular to the plane of the frame. Calculate the torque in N-m required to produce an angular acceleration of \dfrac{\pi}{2}\ rads^{-2}$.
questions.solution:
The distance of each corner from the centre of the square frame is:

$r = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{0.2}{\sqrt{2}}\text{ m}$

The moment of inertia of the four masses (each of mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$) at the corners about the axis passing through the centre and perpendicular to the plane is:

$I_{\text{corners}} = 4 \times m r^2 = 4 \times 2 \times \left(\dfrac{0.2}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2$

$I_{\text{corners}} = 8 \times \dfrac{0.04}{2} = 0.16\text{ kg m}^2$

The $40\text{ kg}$ mass is placed exactly at the centre $O$ (on the axis of rotation), so its distance from the axis is zero. Its moment of inertia is:

$I_{\text{centre}} = 40 \times 0^2 = 0$

The total moment of inertia of the system is:

$I = I_{\text{corners}} + I_{\text{centre}} = 0.16 + 0 = 0.16\text{ kg m}^2$

Given the angular acceleration $\alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ rad s}^{-2}$, the required torque $\tau$ is:

$\tau = I\alpha = 0.16 \times \dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0.08\pi\text{ N-m}$

Expressing this as a fraction:

$\tau = \dfrac{8\pi}{100} = \dfrac{2\pi}{25}\text{ N-m}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2\pi}{25}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A motor bike is moving with a speed of $36 \mathrm{ km} / \mathrm{h}$ along a straight road. The radius of its wheel and its moment of inertia about the axis of rotation are 40 cm and $5 \mathrm{ kg} \mathrm{ m}^2$ respectively. What is the magnitude of the torque applied by the brake to the wheel so as to stop the bike in 10 s?
questions.solution:
The speed of the motorbike is $v = 36 \text{ km/h} = 36 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m/s} = 10 \text{ m/s}$.

The radius of the wheel is $r = 40 \text{ cm} = 0.4 \text{ m}$.

The angular velocity of the wheel is $\omega = \dfrac{v}{r} = \dfrac{10}{0.4} = 25 \text{ rad/s}$.

The wheel is to be stopped in $t = 10 \text{ s}$, so the final angular velocity is $\omega_f = 0$. The angular acceleration $\alpha$ is given by $\alpha = \dfrac{\omega_f - \omega}{t} = \dfrac{0 - 25}{10} = -2.5 \text{ rad/s}^2$.

The magnitude of the angular acceleration is $|\alpha| = 2.5 \text{ rad/s}^2$.

The torque $\tau$ applied by the brake is given by $\tau = I |\alpha|$, where $I = 5 \text{ kg m}^2$.

Substituting the values, $\tau = 5 \times 2.5 = 12.5 \text{ kg m}^2 \texts^{-2}$.

Answer: $12.5 \mathrm{ kg} \mathrm{ m}^2 \mathrm{ s}^{-2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A rigid body is said to be in rotational equilibrium:
options: If the net external torque acting on the body is zero
If the net external force acting on the body is zero
If the net internal force acting on the body is zero
If the net angular momentum of the body is zero
questions.solution:
A rigid body is in rotational equilibrium when it does not undergo any angular acceleration. According to Newton's second law for rotation, the net external torque $\vec{\tau}_{ext}$ acting on a body is equal to the rate of change of its angular momentum, given by $\vec{\tau}_{ext} = \dfrac{d\vec{L}}{dt}$.

For rotational equilibrium, the angular acceleration $\alpha$ must be zero, which implies that the net external torque acting on the body must be zero, i.e., $\sum \vec{\tau}_{ext} = 0$.

The condition of net external force being zero corresponds to translational equilibrium, not rotational equilibrium.

Answer: If the net external torque acting on the body is zero

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Applying a constant torque the speed of a flywheel is increased from 1800 rpm to 2400 rpm in 10 seconds. The number of revolutions made by the flywheel during this time is:
questions.solution:
Initial angular velocity $\omega_0 = 1800 \text{ rpm} = \dfrac{1800 \times 2\pi}{60} \text{ rad/s} = 60\pi \text{ rad/s}$.

Final angular velocity $\omega = 2400 \text{ rpm} = \dfrac{2400 \times 2\pi}{60} \text{ rad/s} = 80\pi \text{ rad/s}$.

Time interval $t = 10 \text{ s}$.

Assuming constant angular acceleration $\alpha$, the average angular velocity is $\omega_{avg} = \dfrac{\omega_0 + \omega}{2} = \dfrac{60\pi + 80\pi}{2} = 70\pi \text{ rad/s}$.

Total angular displacement $\theta = \omega_{avg} \times t = 70\pi \times 10 = 700\pi \text{ radians}$.

The number of revolutions $N$ is given by $\theta = N \times 2\pi$.

$N = \dfrac{\theta}{2\pi} = \dfrac{700\pi}{2\pi} = 350$.

Answer: $350$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A point marked on a ring of radius 2 cm is in contact with a horizontal plane. Now the ring is rolled forward half a revolution along the positive X - direction. Then the angle made by the displacement vector of the point with the X - axis is:
questions.solution:
Let the radius of the ring be $R = 2$ cm. Initially, the point is at the origin $(0, 0)$ in contact with the horizontal plane (X-axis).

The ring rolls forward by half a revolution. The distance moved by the center of the ring is $d = R \times \theta_{rot} = R \times \pi = 2\pi$.

After half a revolution, the center of the ring is at $(2\pi, 2)$. The point, which was initially at the bottom, is now at the top of the ring. The coordinates of the point after half a revolution are $(2\pi, 2R) = (2\pi, 4)$.

The displacement vector $\vec{S}$ of the point from its initial position $(0, 0)$ to its final position $(2\pi, 4)$ is $\vec{S} = (2\pi - 0)\hat{i} + (4 - 0)\hat{j} = 2\pi\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}$.

The angle $\theta$ made by the displacement vector with the X-axis is given by $\tan \theta = \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{4}{2\pi} = \dfrac{2}{\pi}$.

Therefore, $\theta = \tan ^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right)$.

Answer: $\theta=\tan ^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A force of $-F\hat{i}$ acts at the origin of the coordinate system. The torque about the point $(0,1,-1)$ is:
questions.solution:
The torque $\vec{\tau}$ about a point $P$ due to a force $\vec{F}$ acting at a point $A$ is given by $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$, where $\vec{r}$ is the position vector of the point of application $A$ relative to the point $P$.

The point of application is $A = (0, 0, 0)$.

The point about which torque is calculated is $P = (0, 1, -1)$.

The position vector $\vec{r}$ of $A$ relative to $P$ is $\vec{r} = \vec{A} - \vec{P} = (0 - 0)\hat{i} + (0 - 1)\hat{j} + (0 - (-1))\hat{k} = -\hat{j} + \hat{k}$.

The force vector is $\vec{F} = -F\hat{i}$.

The torque is $\vec{\tau} = (-\hat{j} + \hat{k}) \times (-F\hat{i}) = F(\hat{j} \times \hat{i}) - F(\hat{k} \times \hat{i})$.

Using the cross product relations $\hat{j} \times \hat{i} = -\hat{k}$ and $\hat{k} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j}$, we get $\vec{\tau} = F(-\hat{k}) - F(\hat{j}) = -F(\hat{j} + \hat{k})$.

Answer: $-F(\hat{\jmath}+\mathrm{k})$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
$O$ is the centre of an equilateral triangle $A B C$. $F_1, F_2$ and $F_3$ are three forces acting along the sides $A B, B C$ and $A C$ as shown in figure.


What should be the magnitude of $F_3$, so that the total torque about $O$ is zero?
questions.solution:
For total torque about $O$ to be zero,

$\begin{array}{rlrl} & & F_1 r+F_2 r-F_3 r & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & F_3 & =F_1+F_2\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Let $I_A$ and $I_B$ be moments of inertia of a body about two axes $A$ and $B$, respectively. The axis $A$ passes through the centre of mass of the body but $B$ does not, then.
options: $I_A < I_B$, whether the axes are parallel or not parallel
if the axes are parallel $I_A < I_B$
if the axes are not parallel $I_A \geq I_B$
questions.solution:
$I_{\mathrm{CM}}$ is less than $I$ about any other axis not passing through centre of mass but only when two axes are parallel.
$\Rightarrow \quad I_B=I_A+I_A r^2$
where, $r$ is the distance between parallel axes.
$\therefore \quad I_A < I_B$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A record player is spinning at an angular velocity of $45 \mathrm{ rpm}$ just before it is turned off. It then decelerates at a constant rate of $0.8 \mathrm{ rad} \mathrm{ s}^{-1}$. The angular displacement is
questions.solution:
The initial angular velocity $\omega_0$ is given as $45 \text{ rpm}$. Converting this to $\text{rad s}^{-1}$:

$\omega_0 = 45 \times \dfrac{2\pi}{60} \text{ rad s}^{-1} = \dfrac{45 \times 2\pi}{60} \text{ rad s}^{-1} = 1.5\pi \text{ rad s}^{-1} \approx 4.712 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$.

The deceleration $\alpha$ is $0.8 \text{ rad s}^{-2}$. Since it is decelerating, $\alpha = -0.8 \text{ rad s}^{-2}$. The final angular velocity $\omega$ when the record player stops is $0 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$.

Using the kinematic equation $\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angular displacement:

$0 = (1.5\pi)^2 + 2(-0.8)\theta$

$1.6\theta = (1.5\pi)^2$

$1.6\theta = 2.25 \times \pi^2$

Taking $\pi^2 \approx 9.8696$:

$1.6\theta = 2.25 \times 9.8696 = 22.2066$

$\theta = \dfrac{22.2066}{1.6} = 13.879 \text{ rad} \approx 13.88 \text{ rad}$.

Answer: 13.88 rad

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular disc of mass $20 \mathrm{ kg}$, having radius $10 \mathrm{ cm}$ is suspended by a wire attached to its centre. The wire is twisted by rotating the disc and released. The time period of torsional oscillations is found to be $1 \mathrm{ s}$. The torsional spring constant of the wire is
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia $I$ of a circular disc about its central axis is given by $I = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$.

Given $M = 20 \text{ kg}$ and $R = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$, we have $I = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times (0.1)^2 = 10 \times 0.01 = 0.1 \text{ kg m}^2$.

The time period $T$ of torsional oscillations is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{C}}$, where $C$ is the torsional spring constant.

Squaring both sides, $T^2 = 4\pi^2 \dfrac{I}{C}$, which implies $C = \dfrac{4\pi^2 I}{T^2}$.

Substituting the given values $T = 1 \text{ s}$ and $I = 0.1 \text{ kg m}^2$:

$C = 4 \times (3.14)^2 \times 0.1 = 4 \times 9.8596 \times 0.1 = 3.94384 \text{ N m rad}^{-1}$.

Rounding to two decimal places, $C \approx 3.94 \text{ N m rad}^{-1}$.

Answer: $3.94 \mathrm{ N m} \mathrm{ rad}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An object of mass $1 \mathrm{ kg}$ is allowed to hang tangentially from the rim of the wheel of radius R. When released from the rest, the block falls vertically through $4 \mathrm{ m}$ height in 2 seconds. The moment of inertia is $1 \mathrm{ kg} \mathrm{ m}^2$. The radius of the wheel $\mathrm{R}$ is
questions.solution:
Let $m = 1 \text{ kg}$ be the mass of the block, $I = 1 \text{ kg m}^2$ be the moment of inertia of the wheel, $R$ be the radius of the wheel, and $h = 4 \text{ m}$ be the distance fallen in time $t = 2 \text{ s}$.

The block starts from rest, so the distance fallen is given by $h = \dfrac{1}{2} a t^2$, where $a$ is the linear acceleration of the block.

$4 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times a \times (2)^2 \Rightarrow 4 = 2a \Rightarrow a = 2 \text{ m/s}^2$.

The equation of motion for the block is $mg - T = ma$, where $T$ is the tension in the string.

$1 \times 9.8 - T = 1 \times 2 \Rightarrow T = 9.8 - 2 = 7.8 \text{ N}$.

The torque $\tau$ on the wheel is $\tau = T \times R = I \alpha$, where $\alpha$ is the angular acceleration of the wheel. Since the string does not slip, $a = R \alpha$, so $\alpha = \dfrac{a}{R}$.

$T \times R = I \times \dfrac{a}{R} \Rightarrow T = \dfrac{I a}{R^2}$.

Substituting the known values: $7.8 = \dfrac{1 \times 2}{R^2} \Rightarrow R^2 = \dfrac{2}{7.8} \approx 0.256$.

Using $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$ as a standard approximation in such problems: $10 - T = 2 \Rightarrow T = 8 \text{ N}$.

$8 = \dfrac{1 \times 2}{R^2} \Rightarrow R^2 = \dfrac{2}{8} = 0.25 \Rightarrow R = 0.5 \text{ m}$.

Answer: 0.5 m

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid cylinder of mass $2 \mathrm{ kg}$ and radius $0.2 \mathrm{ m}$ is rotating about its own axis without friction with angular velocity $5 \mathrm{ rad} \mathrms^{-1}$. A particle of mass $1 \mathrm{ kg}$ moving with a velocity of $5 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$ strikes the cylinder and sticks to it as shown in figure. The angular velocity of the system after the particle sticks to it will be
questions.solution:
The initial angular momentum of the system about the axis of rotation is the sum of the angular momentum of the cylinder and the angular momentum of the particle. The cylinder is rotating about its own axis, so its angular momentum is $L_{cyl} = I \omega = (\dfrac{1}{2} M R^2) \omega$.

Given $M = 2 \text{ kg}$, $R = 0.2 \text{ m}$, and $\omega = 5 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$, we have $I = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times (0.2)^2 = 0.04 \text{ kg m}^2$. Thus, $L_{cyl} = 0.04 \times 5 = 0.2 \text{ kg m}^2 \texts^{-1}$.

The particle of mass $m = 1 \text{ kg}$ moves with velocity $v = 5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ at a perpendicular distance $R = 0.2 \text{ m}$ from the axis. Its angular momentum is $L_{part} = m v R = 1 \times 5 \times 0.2 = 1.0 \text{ kg m}^2 \texts^{-1}$.

The total initial angular momentum is $L_{initial} = L_{cyl} + L_{part} = 0.2 + 1.0 = 1.2 \text{ kg m}^2 \texts^{-1}$.

After the particle sticks to the cylinder, the new moment of inertia is $I' = I + m R^2 = 0.04 + 1 \times (0.2)^2 = 0.04 + 0.04 = 0.08 \text{ kg m}^2$.

By conservation of angular momentum, $L_{initial} = L_{final} = I' \omega'$.

$1.2 = 0.08 \times \omega'$.

$\omega' = \dfrac{1.2}{0.08} = \dfrac{120}{8} = 15.0 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $15.0 \mathrm{ rad s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass $5 \mathrm{ kg}$ at rest is rotated for $25 \mathrm{ s}$ with a constant moment of force $10 \mathrm{ Nm}$. Find the work done if the moment of inertia of the body is $5 \mathrm{ kg} \mathrm{ m}^2$.
questions.solution:
Given the moment of force (torque) $\tau = 10 \text{ Nm}$, moment of inertia $I = 5 \text{ kg m}^2$, and time $t = 25 \text{ s}$.

The angular acceleration $\alpha$ is given by $\tau = I \alpha$.

$\alpha = \dfrac{\tau}{I} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2 \text{ rad/s}^2$.

Since the body starts from rest, the initial angular velocity $\omega_0 = 0$. The angular velocity after time $t$ is $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t = 0 + 2 \times 25 = 50 \text{ rad/s}$.

The work done is equal to the change in rotational kinetic energy $W = \Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2 - \dfrac{1}{2} I \omega_0^2$.

$W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times (50)^2 - 0 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 2500 = 5 \times 1250 = 6250 \text{ J}$.

Answer: 6250 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin circular ring of mass $M$ and radius $R$ rotates about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its plane, with a constant angular velocity $\omega$. Four small spheres each of mass $m$ (negligible radius) are kept gently to the opposite ends of two mutually perpendicular diameters of the ring. The new angular velocity of the ring will be
questions.solution:
According to conservation of angular momentum,
$I \omega=\text{ constant } 
i.e. we can write,
 \begin{array}{rlrl}
I_1 \omega_1 & =I_2 \omega_2 & \\
\text{ or } & M R^2 \omega =(M+4 m) R^2 \omega_2 & \\
\text{ or } & \omega_2 =\left(\frac{M}{M+4 m}\right) \omega &
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wheel is free to rotate about a horizontal axis through O. A force of $200 \mathrm{ N}$ is applied at a point $\mathrm{P} 2 \mathrm{ cm}$ from the center $\mathrm{O}$. OP makes an angle of $55^{{}^{\circ}}$ with $\mathrm{x}$ axis and the force is in the plane of the wheel making an angle of $25^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the horizontal axis. What is the torque?
questions.solution:
The torque $\vec{\tau}$ is defined as $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$, where $\vec{r}$ is the position vector of the point of application P relative to the axis O, and $\vec{F}$ is the applied force.

The magnitude of the torque is given by $\tau = r F \sin \theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the position vector $\vec{r}$ and the force vector $\vec{F}$.

Given $r = 2 \text{ cm} = 0.02 \text{ m}$ and $F = 200 \text{ N}$.

The position vector $\vec{r}$ makes an angle of $55^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the x-axis. The force vector $\vec{F}$ makes an angle of $25^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the horizontal (x-axis).

The angle $\theta$ between $\vec{r}$ and $\vec{F}$ is the difference between their angles with the horizontal axis: $\theta = 55^{{}^{\circ}} - 25^{{}^{\circ}} = 30^{{}^{\circ}}$.

Substituting the values into the torque formula:

$\tau = (0.02 \text{ m}) \times (200 \text{ N}) \times \sin(30^{{}^{\circ}})$

$\tau = 4 \times 0.5 = 2 \text{ N m}$.

Answer: 2 N m

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin circular ring of mass ,$M$ and radius $R$ rotates about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its plane, with a constant angular velocity $\omega$. Four small spheres each of mass $m$ (negligible radius) are kept gently to the opposite ends of two mutually perpendicular diameters of the ring. The new angular velocity of the ring will be
questions.solution:
The initial moment of inertia of the ring about the axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is $I_1 = MR^2$.

The initial angular momentum of the system is $L = I_1 \omega = MR^2 \omega$.

When four small spheres of mass $m$ are placed at the ends of two mutually perpendicular diameters, they are at a distance $R$ from the axis of rotation. The new moment of inertia of the system becomes $I_2 = MR^2 + 4(mR^2) = (M + 4m)R^2$.

Since no external torque acts on the system, the angular momentum is conserved, so $L_1 = L_2$.

$MR^2 \omega = (M + 4m)R^2 \omega'$, where $\omega'$ is the new angular velocity.

Solving for $\omega'$, we get $\omega' = \dfrac{MR^2 \omega}{(M + 4m)R^2} = \left( \dfrac{M}{M + 4m} \right) \omega$.

Answer: $\left(\dfrac{M}{M+4 m}\right) \omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A disc of moment of inertia $4 \mathrm{ kg}-\mathrm{m}^2$ revolving with $16 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$ is placed on another disc of moment of inertia $8 \mathrm{Kg}-\mathrm{m}^2$ revolving $4 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$. The angular frequency of composite disc
questions.solution:
The principle of conservation of angular momentum states that the total angular momentum of the system remains constant when no external torque acts on it.

Let $I_1 = 4 \text{ kg-m}^2$ and $\omega_1 = 16 \text{ rad/s}$ be the moment of inertia and angular velocity of the first disc.

Let $I_2 = 8 \text{ kg-m}^2$ and $\omega_2 = 4 \text{ rad/s}$ be the moment of inertia and angular velocity of the second disc.

The initial total angular momentum $L_i$ is given by $L_i = I_1 \omega_1 + I_2 \omega_2$.

$L_i = (4 \times 16) + (8 \times 4) = 64 + 32 = 96 \text{ kg-m}^2/\text{s}$.

When the two discs are placed together, they form a composite disc with a total moment of inertia $I = I_1 + I_2 = 4 + 8 = 12 \text{ kg-m}^2$.

Let $\omega$ be the final angular velocity of the composite disc. The final angular momentum $L_f$ is $L_f = (I_1 + I_2) \omega = 12 \omega$.

Equating $L_i = L_f$, we get $96 = 12 \omega$.

Solving for $\omega$, we have $\omega = \dfrac{96}{12} = 8 \text{ rad/s}$.

Answer: $8 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Four particles each of the mass $m$ are placed at the corners of a square of side length $l$. The radius of gyration of the system about an axis perpendicular to the square and passing through its centre is
questions.solution:
The given situation is shown in figure.

Moment of inertia of the systems about an axis perpendicular to the square and passing through the centre is given as $\begin{aligned} I &=m\left(\frac{l}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2}+ m\left(\frac{l}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2}+ m\left(\frac{l}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2}+ m\left(\frac{l}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2}\\ &=4 \frac{m l^{2}}{2}=2 m l^{2} \end{aligned} If $ k$ be the radius of gyration, then I=4 m k^{2} $\therefore From $Eegs. (i) und (ii), we have \begin{aligned}2 m l^{2} &=4 m k^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad k &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform circular disc of mass $400 \mathrm{ g}$ and radius $4.0 \mathrm{ cm}$ is rotated about one of its diameter at an angular speed of $10 \mathrm{rot} / \mathrm{s}$. The kinetic energy of the disc is
questions.solution:
Given, mass of disc, $M=400 \mathrm{ g}=0.4 \mathrm{ kg}$
Radius, $R=4 \mathrm{ cm}=4 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{ m}$
Angular speed, $\omega=2 \pi \times 10$
=20 $\pi \mathrm{rad}$/ $\mathrm{s}\therefore$ Moment of inertia of disc about its diameter I_{d}=$\frac{1}{4}$ M R^{2} $\therefore$ Kinetic energy of disc $\begin{aligned}&=\frac{1}{2} I_{d} \omega^{2}\\
&=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} M R^{2} \times \omega^{2}=\frac{1}{8} M R^{2} \omega^{2}\\
&=\frac{1}{8} \times0.4 \times\left(4 \times10^{-2}\right)^{2}\times(20 \pi)^{2}\\
&=3.2 \times10^{-1} \mathrm{ J}
\end{aligned}$ Hence, no option is correct.

questions.q: A person sitting firmly over a rotating stool has his arms stretched. If he folds his arms, his angular momentum about the axis of the rotation
questions.solution: According to conservation of angular momentum, when no external torque is applied on the rotating system, then its angular momentum remains unchanged.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The diagram shows a barrel of weight $1.0 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{ N}$ on a frictionless slope inclined at $30^{{}^{\circ}}$ to the horizontal.

The force is parallel to the slope. What is the work done in moving the barrel a distance of $5.0 \mathrm{ m}$ up the slope?
questions.solution:
The given situation is shown below

Work done in moving the barrel on the frictionless slope is equal to change in potential energy. i.e. $W=m g\left(h_{1}-h_{2}\right)$ Here, $\quad m g=1 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~N}$ From figure, $\sin 30^{\circ}=\frac{h_{1}-h_{2}}{5}$ $\Rightarrow \quad h_{1}-h_{2}=5 \sin 30^{\circ}=\frac{5}{2}=25 \mathrm{~m}$ Putting these values in Eq. (i), we get $$ W=1 \times 10^{3}(2.5)=2.5 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~J} $$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A mass of $0.1 \mathrm{ kg}$ is hung at the $20 \mathrm{ cm}$ mark from a $1 \mathrm{ m}$ rod weighing $0.25 \mathrm{ kg}$ pivoted at its centre. The rod will not topple if
options: No other mass is attached to the rod
$0.15 \mathrm{ kg}$ is hung at $80 \mathrm{ cm}$ mark
$0.15 \mathrm{ kg}$ is hung at $70 \mathrm{ cm}$ mark
$0.10 \mathrm{ kg}$ is hung at $70 \mathrm{ cm}$ mark
questions.solution:
Given, $m=0.1 \mathrm{ kg}$

Let $x$ be the position of mass of $0.1 \mathrm{ kg}$ from its centre and $x^{\prime}$ be the position of second mass $m_{2}$ that must be suspended to the other end to prevent the rod from toppling. So, x=50-20=30 $\mathrm{ cm}=0.3 \mathrm{ m}$ The rod will not topple if net torque on it is zero. So, balancing the moments about its centre, we get $m_{1} g x=m_{2} g x^{\prime}\Rightarrow \quad m_{2} x=0.1 \times 0.3=0.03 \mathrm{ kg}-\mathrm{m}$ From options, it is possible only in case of $(\mathrm{c})$. $m_{2}=0.15 \mathrm{ kg}x^{\prime}=\frac{0.03}{0.15}=0.2 \mathrm{ m}=20 \mathrm{ cm}\therefore$ The second mass of $0.15 \mathrm{ kg}$ should be hanged at $(50+20=) 70 \mathrm{ cm}$ mark.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ring rolls down an inclined plane. The ratio of the rotational kinetic energy to translational kinetic energy is
questions.solution:
The rotational kinetic energy of a ring is K_{R}=$\frac{1}{2}$ I $\omega^{2}$ For a ring, $\quad {I}=M R^{2}$ and $\omega=\frac{v}{R}$
\therefore \quad K_{R}=$\frac{1}{2} \left(M R^{2}\right)\times\left(\frac{v}{R}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}M v^{2} Also, translational kinetic energy, K_{T}=\frac{1}{2}$ M v^{2}$
\therefore K_{R}=K_{T} \text{ or }K_{R}: K_{T}=1: 1
$
